extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions, where each example consists of a question, a Wikipedia paragraph, the article title, and a yes/no answer.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were gathered using the Natural Questions pipeline with an added filter for yes/no questions. Questions came from anonymized, aggregated Google search queries, were heuristically identified as likely yes/no questions, retained only when a Wikipedia page appeared in the top five results, and then sent to human annotators who judged question quality, found an answer-containing passage, marked unanswerable cases, and labeled the answer yes or no.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators could mark questions as not answerable when the Wikipedia article did not contain the requested information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated Google search queries and Wikipedia pages/articles.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset keeps only questions marked as having a yes/no answer and pairs each question with the selected passage rather than the full document. It also combines 13k newly gathered questions with 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set, then splits them into train/dev/test with all NQ questions placed in train.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries likely to be yes/no questions were heuristically identified by selecting queries whose first word was in a manually constructed indicator-word set and that were of sufficient length. Only questions with a Wikipedia result in the top five were kept.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotators labeled question/article pairs in three steps: determine whether the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, factual), find a passage containing enough information to answer it or mark it not answerable, and finally label the answer as yes or no.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotation quality was assessed by having three authors label 110 randomly chosen examples and resolve disagreements by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels. The original answer annotations achieved 90% accuracy against these gold labels; disagreements included six ambiguous/debatable cases and five annotator misunderstandings. Because agreement was sufficiently high, the released train/dev/test sets use single annotations per example.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Three of the annotators used for quality assessment were the paper's authors.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Heuristic filtering using a manually constructed set of indicator words to identify likely yes/no queries.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Search queries from users were used in anonymized, aggregated form.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support models for the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions and to build datasets tied to clear end-user applications rather than artificial settings.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset has a class imbalance toward yes answers, and question topics are skewed toward entertainment media and other popular topics. The paper also notes some passage-only signal correlated with yes answers.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset uses singly annotated examples, some annotations are ambiguous or erroneous, and the task is limited to passage-level rather than document-level evidence. The authors note the dataset analysis may be slightly out of date after updates.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Reading comprehension and yes/no question answering; used for training, development, and testing models. The paper uses a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: First, in order to assess annotation quality, three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement. We call the resulting labels “gold-standard” labels. On the 110 selected examples, the answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where the answer annotation differed from the gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Since the agreement was sufficiently high, we elected to use singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets

rai:dataBiases.evidence: “Yes” answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set)... The pre-trained BERT Lmodel reached 64.48% dev set accuracy using just the question and 66.74% using just the passage... this suggests there is little signal in the question by itself, but that some language pattems in the passage correlate with the answer.
